writing.explanation:
With choices [0,1,1,3], index 0 selects 10, index 1 selects 20, index 2 retains 20, and index 3 selects 40. Each index i replaces with probability 1/(i+1); the exact replacement rule is now explicit.

The worked program is a complete executable for this pattern. Its core function uses typed input so the state transitions remain visible. The challenge input contract is: Parse equally sized values and choices arrays. At zero-based index i, choices[i] is in 0..=i; replace the one-item reservoir exactly when choices[i] == i. Return the selected value, or none for empty arrays. The visible fixture is `values=[10,20,30,40]; choices=[0,1,1,3]` and its example result is `40`. The implementation and additional semantic fixtures were checked against an independent reference calculation. Those bounded tests establish these examples; they are not a proof for all inputs or a measurement on an iPhone.

Return a canonical String from solve: lowercase true/false for booleans; decimal integers without extra signs, leading zeros or whitespace; comma-separated sequence values and semicolon-separated groups. Whole-number medians have no decimal suffix; half medians use .5. Do not append a newline to the returned value. Preserve the explicitly named textual sentinels such as none or #. Input fixtures are bounded so the demonstrated arithmetic fits its named Rust types; satisfy the stated input preconditions before applying the algorithm.

String and character-grid fixtures use ASCII unless the lesson explicitly specifies Unicode scalar values.

Begin with the concrete question: Parse equally sized values and choices arrays. At zero-based index i, choices[i] is in 0..=i; replace the one-item reservoir exactly when choices[i] == i. Return the selected value, or none for empty arrays. For the visible input `values=[10,20,30,40]; choices=[0,1,1,3]`, the stated result is `40`. Before reading code, name the smallest piece of information that must survive from one step to the next. A scan turns a sequence into a small piece of state. Say what the state means after the first i elements, before you describe a loop body. That is the mental model for Reservoir Sampling; it gives you a reason for each update instead of a line of code to memorise.

The core mechanism is this: Replace a fixed reservoir with decreasing probability while streaming unknown-length input. Treat it as a claim to test after every operation. Write down the state before the first operation, update it once, and ask which part of the claim is still true. If an item is skipped, inserted, or removed, explain why that action cannot destroy an answer that should be retained. A useful trace has columns for the current input position, the state before the step, the action, and the state afterward. Use the visible sample until the expected result becomes inevitable rather than merely plausible.

Finally justify the stated bound, O(n) time · O(1) reservoir state for k=1. Count how often an item, edge, state, or candidate can enter the main operation; do not infer the bound from the number of loop keywords alone. Use an empty slice and a one-element slice as checks. Initial values must not silently assume that at least one item exists. Predict the result for a smallest legal input and for one case that stresses the invariant. If your prediction disagrees with a hand trace, repair the state definition before changing code.
